p: When a small business decides it needs something that works well on phones, the question quickly becomes whether to build a native app for the app stores or a progressive web app that runs in the browser. The answer affects cost, time to launch, what the app can do and how much work it is to maintain for years afterwards.

This guide explains what each approach is, where each one shines, where it struggles, and how to choose based on your real needs rather than on trends. It goes beyond the general question of web versus mobile and focuses on progressive web apps, since they are often overlooked by business owners even though they suit many practical use cases.

h: What is a progressive web app?
p: A progressive web app, or PWA, is a website built with a few extra technologies that make it behave much like an installed app. It is delivered over a secure connection, has a manifest file that describes its name, icon and colours, and uses a service worker, a script that runs in the background and can cache files so parts of the app work offline or on a poor connection.

Users can open it from a link, and on supported devices they can add it to their home screen where it launches in its own window without the browser address bar. You build and maintain one codebase that works on phones, tablets and computers, and updates reach everyone as soon as you publish them, with no store approval step.

A native app is built specifically for one operating system, usually Android or iOS, using that platform's tools and languages, and installed from an app store. Cross-platform frameworks such as React Native or Flutter let a team share much of the code between Android and iOS while still producing real store apps, which sits between the two extremes.

Native apps can use the full range of device capabilities and system integrations, tend to offer the smoothest performance for demanding tasks, and benefit from the visibility and trust of store listings. The trade-off is more development and maintenance effort, store review processes and, for separate native versions, building and testing the app twice.

list: One codebase for every device: a single team and a single release process serve Android, iOS, tablets and desktops.
No store gatekeeping: you can ship fixes the same day without waiting for review, and users never need to update manually.
Instant reach: people can start using the app from a link, a QR code or a search result without installing anything.
Lower cost to build and maintain, particularly for content, forms, bookings and business tools.
Good for offline basics: caching can let customers browse a menu or let staff view their schedule when the signal drops.
Search visibility: because it is a website, its pages can be found through search engines, unlike content hidden inside a store app.

h: Where native apps are the better choice
list: Deep hardware access: advanced Bluetooth use, background location tracking, sensors, NFC and complex camera features are generally more dependable in native apps.
Demanding performance: games, heavy graphics, augmented reality and intensive on-device processing.
Store presence: some audiences expect to find you in the app store, and store listings can support promotion and trust.
System integration: widgets, wallet passes, deep operating-system features and background tasks that must run reliably.
Consistent notifications and engagement tools across platforms where web support is limited.

h: Check support on the devices your customers actually use
p: Browser and operating-system support for PWA features is not identical everywhere, and it changes over time. Installing to the home screen, push notifications, background sync and access to certain device features have historically worked differently on Android and iOS. A feature that works well in your Android test may behave differently on an iPhone.

The practical advice is to list the exact features your app needs, check the current support for them on the browsers and devices of your real customers, and test on actual phones before committing. If a must-have feature is unreliable on a major platform, that is a strong signal to consider a native or cross-platform approach for that part.

h: A worked example: a field-service tool for a cleaning company
p: Imagine a cleaning company with twenty staff who visit different client sites each day. The owner wants staff to see their daily schedule, tick off tasks, add notes and photos, and have the office see progress in real time. Staff use a mix of personal phones, and some sites have weak signal.

A PWA looks attractive here. It runs on every phone without app store accounts, new staff can start by opening a link, and updates are immediate. Caching lets staff view the schedule offline, and queued updates can be sent when the connection returns. Photo upload from the camera is supported in modern browsers. The company would still test on the phones its staff actually carry, and would check whether any needed feature, such as precise background location tracking, is a requirement. If it is, a native or cross-platform app might be needed for that part, while the rest could remain a web app.
This is a fictional scenario, but it shows the right approach: begin from the tasks people must do, then match the technology to them.

list: What must the app do that a website cannot? Write down specific features, not general wishes.
Where will users find it: through links and search, through the app stores, or both?
Which devices do they use, and have you tested your key features there?
What is your budget and timeline for the first release and for ongoing maintenance?
How often will it change? Frequent changes favour the instant updates of a web app.

p: You do not have to choose once and forever. A common, sensible path is to start with a PWA to validate the idea quickly and cheaply, learn how people use it, and then build a native or cross-platform app later if the data shows a clear need for store presence or advanced features. Because the backend, the data and much of the design can be reused, the work is not wasted.

Another approach is to wrap an existing web app so that it can be listed in the stores, while still sharing most of the code. Such packaging has its own rules and review requirements, so it is worth discussing with a developer before assuming it will be simple.

list: Choosing native because it sounds more professional, without a feature that actually needs it.
Choosing a PWA without checking support for a must-have feature on iPhones or on older Android devices.
Ignoring offline behaviour. Decide what should work without a connection and test it in airplane mode.
Forgetting security. A PWA must be served over HTTPS and should protect user data like any other application.
Underestimating maintenance: both approaches need regular updates, testing on new devices and security fixes.
List the five most important tasks users must perform on their phones.
Mark any task that needs deep hardware access, background processing or store distribution.
Check current PWA support for those features on your customers' devices.
Decide what must work offline and how data will sync afterwards.
Build a small prototype and test it on real phones in real conditions.
Choose PWA, cross-platform or native, and plan the first release as a minimum viable product.

p: Can a PWA be listed in the app stores? In some cases a PWA can be packaged for stores, but the options and rules differ by platform and change over time. Check the current requirements or ask a developer before relying on this.

Is a PWA cheaper than a native app? Often yes, because there is one codebase and no store process, but the exact difference depends on the features. A complex PWA can cost more than a simple native app, so scope matters more than the label.

Do PWAs work offline? They can, if the developers use a service worker to cache the right files and data. Offline behaviour has to be designed deliberately, including how changes made offline are saved and merged later.

Will my customers know how to install a PWA? Many will not, so you may need a simple prompt or instructions. Many users also simply use it as a website, which is fine because it works in the browser as well.

list: A progressive web app is a secure website with extras that let it install, load quickly and work partly offline.
PWAs suit forms, bookings, content and business tools, offering one codebase, instant updates and low cost.
Native apps are better for deep hardware use, demanding performance and strong store presence.
Support for PWA features varies by platform, so test on the real devices your customers use.
Start from user tasks, and consider a staged path from PWA to native if the need is proven.
